notes: Ruling slot 3 = PR of President Julio César Méndez Montenegro. The PR governed without a formal coalition partner (only its pact with the army); coalition slot 18 holds Manuel Colom Argueta's FUR, the democratic-left heir of the October Revolution. MLN moved from MD slot 20 to slot 1 (pro-US anti-communist right, slot 20 has no starting popularity while the MLN is a major party about to win the March 1970 election). DCG placed in slot 2 following MD's own placement of El Salvador's PDC in Liberals. PID (army party modelled on the PRI) in slot 13. FAR (Castroist, split from the Moscow-line PGT in 1968) in slot 19; MR-13 of Yon Sosa in slot 5. Belize irredentism in slot 20, VP Marroquín Rojas's anti-US nationalists in slot 6.

0.name: Los Coroneles de Zacapa
0.text:
The officers who ran the 1966–68 pacification of Zacapa and Izabal form a tight power bloc around Colonel Carlos Arana Osorio, the ‘Butcher of Zacapa’ to his enemies. Removed from his command and sent as ambassador to Nicaragua in 1968, Arana is back as the presidential candidate of the MLN–PID alliance for the March 1970 election, and his comrades expect the barracks to follow him.

They want a strong, uniformed presidency that finishes the guerrilla war by any means, backed by US advisers, Green Beret training and military aid. Their leverage lies in the eastern garrisons, the military commissioners in the villages and the gratitude of planters who credit them with saving the Oriente.

1.name: Movimiento de Liberación Nacional
1.text:
Heir to Carlos Castillo Armas's 1954 ‘Liberation’ that toppled Jacobo Árbenz, the MLN proudly calls itself the party of organized violence. Led by Mario Sandoval Alarcón, it sits in opposition to the PR government but has joined the army's Institutional Democratic Party behind Colonel Carlos Arana Osorio, the favourite for the March 1970 election.

The MLN stands for uncompromising anti-communism, the defence of private property against any revival of agrarian reform and the closest alignment with Washington. Its base lies in the ladino towns and cattle country of the east, among planters, small-town notables and armed militants, and its leverage comes from its ties to the officer corps and the death squads.

2.name: Democracia Cristiana Guatemalteca
2.text:
Founded in 1955 by Catholic lay activists around René de León Schlotter, the DCG was kept out of the 1966 elections and has since grown into the third force of Guatemalan politics. For the March 1970 vote it fields Jorge Lucas Caballeros, presenting itself as the honest alternative to both the tired PR and the MLN's crusade.

Inspired by Catholic social teaching and the Christian Democratic successes in Chile and Venezuela, it promises cooperatives, rural credit, literacy and a moderate land reform within an anti-communist, pro-Western framework. Its strength lies with Catholic Action catechists in the Maya highlands, urban professionals, students and young priests, though army hostility keeps it far from power.

3.name: Partido Revolucionario
3.text:
Founded in 1957 by Mario Méndez Montenegro as the moderate heir of the 1944 October Revolution, the PR has governed since July 1966 under President Julio César Méndez Montenegro, who took over the candidacy after his brother's death. The price of office was a pact leaving the army a free hand, and the party now runs Mario Fuentes Pieruccini for the March 1970 election.

The PR speaks the language of social reform, labour rights, public works and civilian rule, and keeps close ties to Washington and the Alliance for Progress. Its base is the urban middle class, public employees, teachers and part of organized labour, but years of counter-insurgency under its watch have drained its revolutionary credibility.

4.name: Partido Guatemalteco del Trabajo
4.text:
Guatemala's communist party, founded in 1949 and a partner of the Árbenz government, has been banned since 1954. In March 1966 security forces seized and killed 28 of its leaders and allies, among them the labour veteran Víctor Manuel Gutiérrez, and in 1968 the guerrillas of the FAR broke with it. Secretary-General Bernardo Alvarado Monzón leads the party from the underground.

The PGT follows Moscow's line, combining clandestine union and student work with cautious, conditional support for armed struggle. It seeks a democratic, anti-imperialist and agrarian revolution as the first stage toward socialism. Its leverage rests on cadres in the university, the teachers' and railway unions and old networks of the 1952 land reform.

5.name: Movimiento Revolucionario 13 de Noviembre
5.text:
The MR-13 takes its name from the failed officers' revolt of 13 November 1960 against President Ydígoras Fuentes. Its leader, the US-trained former lieutenant Marco Antonio Yon Sosa, turned the rebels into a peasant guerrilla in the Sierra de las Minas, flirted with Trotskyism in the mid-1960s and survives with small columns battered by the Zacapa offensive.

More radical than the communists, the MR-13 rejects electoral roads and calls for an immediate socialist revolution of workers and peasants, armed land seizures and the expulsion of US influence. Its leverage is meagre: a few dozen fighters, rural sympathizers in the east and the mystique of the guerrilla's founding generation.

6.name: Los de La Hora
6.text:
A loose bloc of conservative nationalists gathers around Vice President Clemente Marroquín Rojas and his combative Guatemala City daily La Hora. The veteran journalist, a fierce anti-communist and an equally fierce critic of Washington, caused a sensation in 1967 by accusing US pilots flying from Panama of bombing Guatemalan territory.

They defend order, property and Catholic tradition but resent US tutelage, the foreign advisers in the barracks, the banana company and every concession on Belize. Their dream is a sovereign, authoritarian Guatemala that picks its friends freely. Influence comes from the newspaper, the vice presidency until July 1970 and sympathy among older officers and provincial notables.

7.name: Los Oficiales de Octubre
7.text:
Behind the army's anti-communist front survives a discreet group of nationalist junior and middle-rank officers who honour the young officers of the 20 October 1944 revolution and the memory of Jacobo Árbenz, now an ageing exile. Since October 1968 the revolutionary military government of General Juan Velasco Alvarado in Peru has given them a new model.

They dream of a disciplined military revolution from above: land reform, nationalization of foreign concessions, an end to US advisers and a foreign policy open to the socialist countries, under firm authoritarian control rather than parties. Their leverage is purely latent, resting on staff colleges, western garrisons and resentment of the oligarchy, and exposure means a bullet.

8.name: Hijos de Jabal Amil
8.text:
A handful of Lebanese Shia families who came to Guatemala as peddlers and now keep fabric and hardware shops in the capital and Quetzaltenango, bound by marriage and remittances to the villages of Jabal Amil in southern Lebanon. They gather in private homes for Ashura readings and follow the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, since 1969 chairman of Lebanon's Supreme Islamic Shia Council.

Their aims are modest and communal: religious education for their children, dignity for a tiny minority and support for Sadr's campaign for the deprived Shia of Lebanon. They steer clear of Guatemala's civil war, and their only leverage is commercial credit and discreet links to Beirut.

9.name: Discípulos de Nayaf
9.text:
A tiny devotional circle of young Lebanese Shia men in Guatemala City who received their religious formation from teachers trained in the seminaries of Najaf in Iraq. They circulate pamphlets and taped sermons that reach them via Beirut and venerate the exiled Iranian Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who has taught in Najaf since 1965 and denounces the Shah.

They reject the quietism of their elders, insist that the learned clergy must guide political life and see both American power and Soviet atheism as enemies of the faith. In Guatemala they have no weight at all; their importance lies only in their contacts with militant clerical networks in Lebanon and Iraq.

10.name: Peregrinos de La Meca
10.text:
A small group of Muslim merchants of Palestinian and Lebanese origin, joined by a few Guatemalan converts, who keep their faith through occasional pilgrimages and literature sent by the Mecca-based Muslim World League. They meet for Friday prayers in a private hall in Guatemala City and look to King Faisal of Saudi Arabia as the guardian of the holy places.

Pious, quietist and loyal to established authority, they preach strict monotheism and obedience to rulers, avoid politics and value the Saudi king's anti-communism. Since the Al-Aqsa fire of August 1969 and the Rabat Islamic summit that followed, they hope Riyadh's growing pan-Islamic largesse will fund a first mosque.

11.name: Llamado del Califato
11.text:
A clandestine reading circle of a few Palestinian students and young shop assistants in Guatemala City who copy and pass on the writings of Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, who founded the Hizb ut-Tahrir in Jerusalem in 1953. The loss of Jerusalem in June 1967 radicalized them and convinced them that the Arab regimes have failed.

They hold that only a restored caliphate uniting all Muslims can liberate Palestine and that nationalism, communism and Western democracy alike are forms of unbelief. They shun Guatemalan politics, dismiss the PLO as secular, and their only significance lies in links to Hizb ut-Tahrir cells in Jordan and Lebanon.

12.name: Círculo de Ginebra
12.text:
A study group of educated Arab-Guatemalan Muslims and a few converts who correspond with the Islamic Centre of Geneva, founded in 1961 by the exiled Egyptian Brotherhood figure Said Ramadan. They read Hasan al-Banna in translation and host the occasional visiting preacher passing through Mexico.

They want an Islamic moral and social renewal through education, charity and preaching, see Islam as a third way between capitalism and communism and favour a reformed society rather than revolution. In Guatemala they keep a low profile and cultivate good relations with the authorities, and their leverage lies in respectable professionals and ties to Brotherhood exiles in Europe.

13.name: Partido Institucional Democrático
13.text:
Created in 1965 under the military government of Colonel Enrique Peralta Azurdia and loosely modelled on Mexico's ruling PRI, the PID is the army's own party, a vehicle for officers, bureaucrats and provincial notables. Its candidate Juan de Dios Aguilar de León lost the 1966 election, but the party survives as a broker and now backs Colonel Carlos Arana Osorio in alliance with the MLN.

The PID preaches order, institutional stability and development led by the state and the officer corps, with little ideology beyond anti-communism. Its strength is patronage: municipal posts, public jobs and the goodwill of the high command, which makes it the indispensable junior partner of whoever the army favours.

14.name: Arquidiócesis de Santiago de Guatemala
14.text:
The Catholic hierarchy of the capital is led by Mario Casariego, archbishop since 1964 and since April 1969 Central America's first cardinal. A Spanish-born conservative, he was briefly kidnapped in a murky affair in March 1968 and has since kept close to the government and the army while restraining the reformist priests and missionaries of the highlands.

The archdiocese stands for public morality, religious education, the family and anti-communism, but also for the Church's independence from parties and foreign tutelage, whether Protestant missions from the United States or Marxist ideas from Cuba. Its leverage is immense: parishes, schools, Catholic Action and the moral authority of the cardinal's word.

15.name: Asociación General de Agricultores
15.text:
Founded in 1920, the AGA speaks for the coffee, sugar, cotton and cattle estates of the Pacific piedmont and the Verapaces, and anchors CACIF, the business coordinating committee formed in 1957. Its families backed the 1954 overthrow of Árbenz's land reform and remain the most powerful private interest in the country.

The AGA defends the plantation economy, seasonal migrant labour from the highlands, low taxes and the absolute inviolability of property, and fights every proposal for income tax or land reform. It backs the army's counter-insurgency and finances the right. Its leverage lies in export earnings, private landholdings and dense family ties to officers, bankers and ministers.

16.name: Centro de Estudios Económico-Sociales
16.english: Center for Economic and Social Studies
16.text:
Founded in 1959 by the engineer and industrialist Manuel Ayau Cordón, the CEES is a small Guatemala City think tank that translates and spreads the ideas of Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek and the Foundation for Economic Education. It runs seminars for young businessmen, publishes pamphlets and courts journalists and university students.

It preaches limited government, sound money, free trade and private enterprise as the true answer to communism, and criticizes not only the left but also the state-heavy developmentalism of the Alliance for Progress and the protectionism of the Central American Common Market. Its leverage lies in persuasive businessmen and a growing circle of disciples among the young elite.

17.name: Operación Poc
17.text:
Launched in the mid-1960s by the American ecologist Anne LaBastille together with Guatemalan wardens and lakeside villagers, Operation Poc fights to save the giant pied-billed grebe of Lake Atitlán, the flightless poc, whose numbers collapsed after black bass were introduced for sport fishing. With official backing it has secured a small refuge on the lake shore.

The campaign defends the reed beds, the lake's water and its fish against careless tourism, chalet building and overfishing, and argues that Atitlán's beauty is a national treasure. It has no party and no ideology beyond conservation, but it is Guatemala's first modern environmental cause, with sympathizers among biologists, tourism officials and the press.

18.name: Frente Unido de la Revolución
18.text:
The FUR gathers the democratic left that refuses both the compromises of the governing PR and the guerrilla road. Its driving force is Manuel Colom Argueta, a young law professor and former student leader who invokes the October Revolution of 1944. Denied legal registration as a party, the movement organizes through civic committees and is preparing Colom's run for mayor of Guatemala City.

It stands for agrarian reform, urban planning, trade-union freedom, an end to death-squad terror and national control over natural resources, keeping its distance from both Washington and Moscow. Its base lies among students, university teachers, professionals and the capital's poorer districts, and its leverage is moral and municipal.

19.name: Fuerzas Armadas Rebeldes
19.text:
Founded in 1962 by rebel officers including Luis Turcios Lima and Marco Antonio Yon Sosa together with the communists, the FAR became Guatemala's main guerrilla army. After Turcios Lima's death in 1966 and the bloody Zacapa campaign it lost its rural fronts, broke with the PGT in early 1968 and shifted to urban warfare, killing US Ambassador John Gordon Mein in August 1968.

Inspired by Cuba and Che Guevara rather than Moscow, the FAR holds that only armed struggle can bring a socialist revolution, rejects electoral politics and targets the army, the death squads and US personnel. Its leverage lies in clandestine cells in the capital, kidnappings and support among radical students.

20.name: Belice es Nuestro
20.text:
Belize, the British colony that Guatemala has claimed since the nineteenth century and that its constitutions declare national territory, is the rallying cry of a noisy nationalist milieu of veterans' clubs, provincial journalists, radio commentators and student patriots. The collapse in 1968 of the mediation by the American lawyer Bethuel Webster has hardened their mood.

They demand the ‘recovery’ of Belize by negotiation or force, denounce London and Washington, and accuse every government of weakness on the question. Hostile to the oligarchy's cosmopolitanism as much as to communism, they blend patriotic fervour with resentment of politicians. Their leverage lies in street demonstrations, the press and officers who dream of a march on Belize.

21.name: Movimiento Anticomunista Nacional Organizado
21.text:
Known from its emblem as the Mano Blanca, the White Hand, MANO appeared in June 1966 as a death squad of MLN militants and army officers, and with its sister groups NOA and CADEG it has spread terror through the east and the capital. Its leaflets name targets; its victims, from peasants to students and lawyers, are found tortured by the roadsides.

MANO preaches total war against communism and treats reformists, Christian democrats and trade unionists as the enemy within. It operates under the protection of the security forces and with the money of landowners. Its leverage is fear itself and its overlap with the MLN, the military commissioners and police intelligence.

22.name: Ejército de Guatemala
22.text:
The armed forces have been the arbiter of Guatemalan politics since they toppled Ydígoras Fuentes in 1963. They allowed the civilian Julio César Méndez Montenegro to take office in 1966 only after he conceded them full control of security, and their counter-insurgency in Zacapa and Izabal, backed by US advisers, broke the rural guerrilla by 1968.

The officer corps sees itself as guardian of the nation against communism, guarantor of order and an engine of development through civic action and road building. It values US aid and training but guards its autonomy fiercely. Its leverage is total: arms, intelligence, the military commissioners and the presidency itself, which every serious candidate must seek through the barracks.

23.name: Reino de Guatemala
23.text:
A small salon of old criollo families in Guatemala City and Antigua, proud descendants of colonial merchants and officials, cultivates the memory of the Kingdom of Guatemala, the Spanish realm that stretched from Chiapas to Costa Rica until 1821. They meet in clubs and confraternities, collect heraldry and colonial art and toast the Spanish Crown.

They regard the republic as a century and a half of caudillos and disorder, admire Franco's Spain and greeted the designation of Prince Juan Carlos as Franco's royal successor in July 1969 as a hopeful sign for the Hispanic world. Their politics are nostalgic and Catholic; their leverage lies only in lineage, wealth and social prestige.
